lines.text: Do you know I was once not very far from seeing--really seeing you?
lines.note: Early Robert remembers almost seeing Elizabeth, the first near-meeting behind their whole story.

lines.text: Is it indeed true that I was so near to the pleasure and honour of making your acquaintance? and can it be true that you look back upon the lost opportunity with any regret?
lines.note: Elizabeth answers Robert's near-miss with wonder at the almost-acquaintance, echoing his first letter.

lines.text: You will never more, I hope, talk of 'the honour of my acquaintance,' but I will joyfully wait for the delight of your friendship, and the spring, and my Chapel-sight after all!
lines.note: Robert turns the near-miss into a promise of spring friendship and the hoped-for Chapel sight.

lines.text: Nay--I must have last word--as all people in the wrong desire to have--and then, no more of the subject.
lines.note: Robert takes the last word because he is in the wrong, acknowledging the hurt he caused Elizabeth.

lines.text: You said I had given you great pain--so long as I stop that, think anything of me you choose or can!
lines.note: Robert asks only that he stop giving Elizabeth pain, a direct apology for his wild words.

lines.text: You will think me the most changeable of all the changeable; but indeed it is not my fault that I cannot, as I wished, receive you on Wednesday.
lines.note: Elizabeth, changeable only by circumstance, postpones their meeting while still hoping to see him.

lines.text: Do tell me what you mean precisely by your 'Bells and Pomegranates' title.
lines.note: Elizabeth asks for the meaning of Robert's 'Bells and Pomegranates' title, their private literary shorthand.

lines.text: I meant the whole should prove at last.
lines.note: Robert says the whole work was meant to prove itself at last, answering Elizabeth's question.

lines.text: 'The Duchess' appears to me more than ever a new-minted golden coin--the rhythm of it answering to your own description, 'Speech half asleep, or song half awake?'
lines.note: Elizabeth praises 'The Duchess' as a new-minted golden coin, showing her close reading of his rhythm.

lines.text: Do you remember how you told me of 'Luria' last year, in one of your early letters?
lines.note: Elizabeth recalls Robert's early letter about 'Luria', a callback to their first months.

lines.text: Can it be the same 'Luria,' I think, that 'golden-hearted Luria,' whom you talked of to me, when you complained of keeping 'wild company,' in the old dear letter?
lines.note: Elizabeth remembers Robert's phrase 'golden-hearted Luria' and applies it to him, not only the hero.

lines.text: You were right to bid me never again wish my poor flowers were ‘diamonds’—you could not, I think, speak so to my heart of any diamonds.
lines.note: Robert accepts Elizabeth's reproof about wishing his flowers were diamonds, turning back to her gift.
